messages.author: 5a1b5a9591c118ef
messages.subject: ggplot2 presentation to non-R users
parts:
Hi list,

I've been asked to give a ~1 hour presentation at VUW on ggplot2 (+R)
to physicists who know nothing about R and care little about advanced
statistics. Most of them would typically use Origin/Excel to plot
graphs; Excel / Matlab / Fortran / C for numerical simulations and
data analysis. Any tips? Drawing from my own learning experience and
interests, I'd like to discuss the following points by means of
minimal visual examples, in a consistent story,

- reproducible graphics. Use scripts as templates that can be re-used
with new data.

- grammar of graphics. Express graphics with a consistent and powerful
language to map data and visual representation.

- interactive data exploration. Using the grammar of graphics,
coordinate transforms, aesthetic mappings and facets,
multi-dimensional data sets can be better explored, more
comprehensively, and rapidly.

- good aesthetic defaults. How ggplot2 has been built with elegant and
faithful graphic data representation in mind. (colour palettes,
scales, automatic legend)

- low level graphics control. Grid primitives, themes, custom grid
plots and viewport integration.

- Good choice of graphic devices. pdf, png, tikz. Animation, rgl.
Multipage output. Sweave.

- Data import and transformation. Custom import function for
text-based data sets in multiple files. Parsing of strings, merging
data sets. Transformation from wide/long format.

- R for numerical calculations. Powerful combination of efficient
mathematical routines (matrix operations, complex algebra, ...) and
rich, expressive language (maximize code reuse, closures and lexical
scope, apply family, ...)

- Extensions to R. Highlight packages: plyr, reshape, Rcpp,
RcppArmadillo, RcppEigen.

- Making packages is easy. Interface with C/Fortran/C++ code.
Namespace control. Documentation, examples integrated.

- Open-source, vibrant community.

I do realise this is too much stuff, especially since I like to
present things as a unified story; any experience on what I should
choose first? There's a tradeoff between getting people's attention on
Yet Another Obscure Programming Language, and showing simple enough
examples that they can actually reproduce, and get started quickly
after the presentation.


Best,

baptiste

messages.author: 598eae3a5857142f
messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 presentation to non-R users
parts:
hi,

skip packages, extensions and open-source/vibrant community.
completely useless IMO in an 1-hour presentation; to beginner
especially. the lack of an open-source community (in terms of the #
of people who commit regularly to ggplot2) might be a deal breaker for
some.

you don't need much R for ggplot2.
i would rather skip as many R related topics so I could take a five
min break after 30 minutes.

devices: just mention there are plenty to chose from, single slide
with 4 icons (pdf, png, tikz, sweave). don't explain the options. the
devices should just put the listener at ease, not more.

"good aesthetic defaults": definitely mention this but chose visual
examples that support it. for example, i don't think that [1] is
necessarily elegant nor good looking.

low level graphics control: not sure about this one. the lack of open
documentation on this might suggest it not being a good idea you
mention it. if it is explained in the book (which i don't own), go
ahead and mention it.

data exploration: i like this a lot. do a live exploration instead of
talking about it.

reproducible graphics: coming from Excel this might be the biggest
advantage of it all, no? question is if it will catch on, your
audience being physicists.

R numerical: mention it but don't go into depth.

also: you forgot to mention the most important aspect of it all:
disadvantages. what are potential deal breakers in ggplot2/R. i would
hate listening to someone for 60 minutes just glowing about a certain
language. don't shit a shitter.

also also: you forgot to mention how to get started (proper books,
tutorials etc). nobody is going to remember your 'highlight packages'
crap. but if your presentation can be used as a 'howto'-list at least
they can extract some value and use your presentation later on too.

Thomas
[1] http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/graphics/4d78a8bbd2d35dd79d5a64d2e1d37551.png

messages.author: 13ff1921a4b26560
messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 presentation to non-R users
parts:
I recently taught a short course on data visualization using the
Deducer package to build plots and explain ggplot2 rather than
starting with the R code. Some concepts were much easier to show
graphically with the Deducer Plot Builder. For example, aesthetics can
be toggled between mapping with visually distinctive blue arrows that
point back to a variable list and setting to constants. The dropdown
menus to change the from the default stat for a particular geom and
vice-versa are also helpful in explaining how to combine the elements
of the grammar. Finally, the tabbed and organized list of labeled
icons for all of the geoms/stats/scales/coords is really helpful since
it can be daunting to remember all of the ggplot2 components (right-
click and go to Get Info to link back to Hadley's ggplot2 help page
for each component).

Since Deducer has dialogues to import data and the spreadsheet-like
object browser for exploring data frames, it makes possible a whole
GUI based workflow for beginners to get started with that doesn't
require learning R syntax. I emphasized that there was always
underlying code (with the option to 'view call') and used that to
segue to a discussion of reproducible scripts, reusing code with new
data, and polishing/exporting plots. I prefer to skip entirely over
qplot() which has fewer advantages for those who have never used
plot() from base graphics. Because it implements almost all of ggplot2
in a well designed graphic user interface, Deducer offers an easy way
to get started and teach the concept of a layered system of graphics
before teaching the structure of the R language and the syntax of
ggplot2. Thanks to Ian and Hadley for putting together this great
extension to ggplot2!

-Allan

messages.author: d674bddd91c6f700
messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 presentation to non-R users
parts:
As a physicist myself, I agree that most of us don't know about R, but I'll dispute your claim we "care little about advanced statistics".  I'm a particle physicist*, and the fundamental data sets we deal with are very, very large - probably beyond the ability of R to deal with gracefully.  My experiment collected a petabyte of data last year.  These days the typical tool used to reduce the data is "root" (root.cern.ch).  I came across an interesting presentation about an interface between R and root at the 2007 useR meeting by Adam Lyon: http://www.r-project.org/conferences/useR-2007/program/presentations/lyon.pdf.  But even if the raw data set starts out enormous, the cuts and selections for a particular analysis will reduce the size greatly.  It might be interesting to anticipate the use of R in a hybrid environment - something like root (or whatever) for dealing with the huge volume of data early in the analysis chain, but with R (and ggplot2) showing up as a tool used later in the analysis.

- Dave

*not really, I'm a high-energy nuclear physicist, but the distinction - though important to me - isn't crucial here.

I meant to say that *the audience* I will address for *that particular

certainly had no intention of making a general claim about physicists;
having worked near astrophysicists for a while I'm aware how
instrumental advanced statistics can be to some of us (and should be
put to better use by others, such as myself).

Best regards,

baptiste

messages.author: d588a03e58ea7e7f
messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 presentation to non-R users
parts:
On 7/30/2011 5:56 PM, baptiste auguie wrote:
> Hi list,
>
> I've been asked to give a ~1 hour presentation at VUW on ggplot2 (+R)
> to physicists who know nothing about R and care little about advanced
> statistics. Most of them would typically use Origin/Excel to plot
> graphs; Excel / Matlab / Fortran / C for numerical simulations and
> data analysis. Any tips? Drawing from my own learning experience and
> interests, I'd like to discuss the following points by means of
> minimal visual examples, in a consistent story,

One thing I didn't see in the list directly is LaTeX integration via
Sweave. As physicists, they will already be conversant in LaTeX and
might appreciate tools that fit in that ecosystem better.

> - reproducible graphics. Use scripts as templates that can be re-used
> with new data.

And reproducible research in general. I have long struggled with the
idea of what a "lab notebook" is in the context of computational
research/analysis. Reproducible research is one answer to this
(probably coupled with version control and possibly some other things,
which get too far afield from your core point).

> - grammar of graphics. Express graphics with a consistent and powerful
> language to map data and visual representation.

This is a very powerful concept that is usable even outside of ggplot/R.
Thinking about presenting data where an aspect (dimension) of the data
is represented by a visual aesthetic, and conversely being able to used
additional aesthetics to represent additional dimensions of the data, is
much different than most approaches. I don't know which other programs
allow, say, shape or color to be determined by another variable. Also,
physicists won't have a problem of thinking about this as a
multi-dimensional display; with two Cartesian dimensions, color and
size, you can display 4 continuous dimensions of data. Faceting in two
directions and point shape give three more discrete dimensions. Vector
fields give effectively two more dimensions.

> - interactive data exploration. Using the grammar of graphics,
> coordinate transforms, aesthetic mappings and facets,
> multi-dimensional data sets can be better explored, more
> comprehensively, and rapidly.

Interesting, but as Thomas pointed out, only if you actually do it
interactively, and I would add with a content relevant data set.

> - good aesthetic defaults. How ggplot2 has been built with elegant and
> faithful graphic data representation in mind. (colour palettes,
> scales, automatic legend)
>
> - low level graphics control. Grid primitives, themes, custom grid
> plots and viewport integration.

I wouldn't spend much time on this. Yes, the defaults are pretty good.
However what is even better is that any can be overridden. The
details of how aren't all that relevant.

> - Good choice of graphic devices. pdf, png, tikz. Animation, rgl.
> Multipage output. Sweave.

<Tongue in cheek>
I don't care how many output formats it can do, so long as it does the
one I need.
</Tongue in cheek>

> - Data import and transformation. Custom import function for
> text-based data sets in multiple files. Parsing of strings, merging
> data sets. Transformation from wide/long format.

Data manipulation and management, especially in a reproducible way. I
don't know how much of a core feature you would want to present versus
just something it can do in the course of other things.

> - R for numerical calculations. Powerful combination of efficient
> mathematical routines (matrix operations, complex algebra, ...) and
> rich, expressive language (maximize code reuse, closures and lexical
> scope, apply family, ...)

Matrix operations rest on LAPACK (not reinventing the wheel when it is
not needed).

> - Extensions to R. Highlight packages: plyr, reshape, Rcpp,
> RcppArmadillo, RcppEigen.
>
> - Making packages is easy. Interface with C/Fortran/C++ code.
> Namespace control. Documentation, examples integrated.
>
> - Open-source, vibrant community.

About these 3 together: Open-source is something they probably already
care about or already decided they don't care about. But the
interesting aspect is that expanding the abilities of R is not limited
to the commercial interests of any one company, but can be done by
anyone who has the need (and, of course, skill). This is where the
interfacing to other languages (either package wrapping around, or
direct calls to and from) is interesting.

> I do realise this is too much stuff, especially since I like to
> present things as a unified story; any experience on what I should
> choose first? There's a tradeoff between getting people's attention on
> Yet Another Obscure Programming Language, and showing simple enough
> examples that they can actually reproduce, and get started quickly
> after the presentation.

This is really your core question: why are you giving the talk? Are you
providing an introduction to a language/system that you would like
people to adopt? Are you trying to give people tools that might be
useful in their work? Are you showing people other tools just so they
know that they exist? Are you trying to improve, either in terms of
ability or efficiency, existing practices? Or another way of thinking
of the question, what do you want people to take away (know or do
differently) from your talk?

I think the two most generalizable topics are reproducible research and
the grammar of graphics. These are not R/ggplot specific (though are
well supported by them) and so can be useful even using other tools.
Unfortunately, the two topics don't necessarily flow together well.

I gave a talk at our local R users group about ggplot; it is at
https://github.com/PortlandRUserGroup/Slides/blob/master/Diggs-ggplot2.pdf
That may or may not be useful to you; the source Rnw file is there too.

Also, you mentioned making your presentation a Sweave/beamer document.
If you do so, one thing to point out is that the presentation is a
reproducible document itself.

> Best,
>
> baptiste

BTW, when I talk about physicists, I am speaking inclusively. I am
(was?) a computational statistical physicist, but now I work as a
biostatistician.

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University
